item.title: Caching Policies based on Object Sizes
item.description: arXiv:2610.21035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate eviction policies that consider the lengths of the objects being cached for different cache sizes (cost) and different workloads. Workloads include the Independent Reference Model and real-world production traces. In particular, hybrid policies are considered for segmented caches. A working-set approximation is developed for SIEVE as well as its length-aware extension.
item.dc:creator: Ridwanul Hasan Tanvir, George Kesidis

item.title: Top-Down Microarchitecture Analysis Without Causal Modelling Is Dangerous!
item.description: arXiv:2610.21387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Top-Down Microarchitecture Analysis (TMA) is the standard for identifying CPU bottlenecks. However, TMA implicitly models performance via a single causal path: Workload(dataset, algorithm) => CPU(CPI) => System(Performance) (microarchitectural efficiency path). It overlooks two hidden causal paths: Workload(dataset, algorithm) => Instructions(Retired) => System(Performance) (algorithmic efficiency path) and Workload(dataset, algorithm) => Instructions(Retired) => CPU(CPI) => System(Performance) (microarchitecture-algorithm efficiency path). This causal blindness often misleads architects into futile hardware optimizations. To address this, we propose Causal Top-Down Microarchitecture Analysis (CTMA). Utilizing the object causal model, CTMA explicitly models these three causal paths among the workload, instructions, CPU, and system. We validate CTMA across Intel, AMD, and ARM platforms. Our experiments reveal counterintuitive insights: (1) CPI Profiling Blindness: Algorithmic instruction bloat can double elapsed time while the CPI profile remains frozen. (2) Over-Speculation Congestion: Throttling the Frontend paradoxically improves performance in pointer-chasing algorithms. (3) ILP Window Collapse: Extreme data topologies shift bottlenecks from Backend ROB capacity to Frontend fill-rate starvation. (4) Op-Cache SMT Overlap: Ultra-small footprints yield SMT speedups on Intel but cause severe thrashing on AMD. (5) "Ghost State" Artifact: Stale pipeline mitigations on Intel Xeon Gold 5120T artificially boost performance by 22.75% on SPEC CPU2017 and 42.2% on SPEC CPU2026. Based on this, we propose a dynamic speculation throttling mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Chenxi Wang, Lei Wang, Wanling Gao, Guoxin Kang, Fanda Fan, Jianfeng Zhan

item.title: TeraAgent: A Distributed Agent-Based Simulation Engine for Simulating Half a Trillion Agents
item.description: arXiv:2509.24063v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agent-based simulation is a method for studying highly complex systems in disciplines as diverse as biology, medicine, sociology, economics, finance, and more. In this method, an agent represents a small part of the system, such as a human cell, and, through interactions among many agents, the system's behavior emerges, like the growth of cancer in the human body. Real-world complex systems, such as a human organ, comprise billions of agents. However, the state-of-the-art agent-based simulation platform, BioDynaMo, does not support the distributed processing of a simulation across servers. This limitation restricts the scalability of agent counts to the computational resources available within a single server, hindering users from conducting larger and more meaningful simulations. In this paper, we introduce TeraAgent, a new distributed agent-based simulation engine. To overcome BioDynaMo's scalability limitation, TeraAgent enables efficient exchange of agent information across servers by implementing two solutions: 1) a tailored serialization mechanism that allows agents to be accessed and mutated directly at the receive buffer, and 2) delta encoding that significantly reduces data transfer across servers by leveraging the iterative nature of agent-based simulations. Built on our solutions, TeraAgent 1) enables extreme-scale simulations with half a trillion agents (292x that of BioDynaMo) on 84,096 CPU cores, 2) reduces time-to-result leveraging parallelism across compute nodes, 3) improves interoperability with third-party tools, and 4) provides users with more hardware flexibility. TeraAgent serializes agents with a median speedup of 110x (37x for deserialization) over the state-of-the-art ROOT I/O baseline, delivers 8x the agent update rate per CPU core of Biocellion, and improves in-situ visualization performance by 39x.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Breitwieser, Ahmad Hesam, Abdullah Giray Ya\u{g}l{\i}k\c{c}{\i}, Mohammad Sadrosadati, Fons Rademakers, Onur Mutlu

item.title: Wattlytics: A Web Platform for Co-Optimizing Performance, Energy, and TCO in HPC Clusters
item.description: arXiv:2604.08182v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The escalating computational demands and energy footprint of GPU-accelerated computing systems complicate informed design and operational decisions. We present the first release of Wattlytics (https://wattlytics.netlify.app), an interactive, browser-based decision-support system. Unlike existing procurement-oriented calculators, Wattlytics uniquely integrates benchmark-driven GPU performance scaling, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-aware piecewise power modeling, and multi-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis within a single interactive environment. Users can configure heterogeneous systems across contemporary GPU architectures (GH200, H100, L40S, L40, A40, A100, and L4), select representative scientific workloads (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER), and explore deployment scenarios under constraints such as energy prices, system lifetime, and frequency scaling. Wattlytics computes multidimensional decision metrics (TCO breakdown, work-per-TCO, power-per-TCO, and work-per-watt-per-TCO) and supports design-space exploration, what-if scenarios, sensitivity metrics (elasticity, Sobol indices, Monte Carlo) and collaborative features to guide realistic cluster design and procurement under uncertainty. We validate the fitted power and performance models and compare four deployment modes: fixed budget, fixed GPU count, fixed performance, and fixed power. Our case studies show that, under budget or energy constraints, optimally deployed energy-efficient GPUs can outperform higher-performance alternatives in overall cost-effectiveness. Wattlytics helps users explore the design parameter space and distinguish between cost- and risk-driving factors, turning HPC design into a well-informed and explainable decision-making process.
item.dc:creator: Ayesha Afzal, Georg Hager, Gerhard Wellein

item.title: Optimal Calibration of Quantum Network Links
item.description: arXiv:2606.18167v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The reliable distribution of entanglement is essential for the effective operation of quantum networks. Due to fundamental differences between quantum and classical communication systems, it is necessary to develop specialised algorithms and protocols that also account for quantum-specific constraints. In this work, we focus on the issue of recalibration. As suggested by recent experimental studies, the process of local entanglement generation in a quantum link degrades over time due to environmental changes that have to be estimated and compensated via a fixed-duration calibration operation, during which the link is not available. Therefore, in such a quantum network, every link alternates between an activation period, during which it operates normally, and a calibration period, during which it cannot participate in the end-to-end entanglement distribution, thereby creating a trade-off between link quality (the initial fidelity of generated pairs, which decays during activation) and availability (the fraction of time the link is usable, which calibration reduces). We develop analytically a protocol for optimally assigning activation periods to each link in linear quantum repeater chains, subject to any general end-to-end fidelity requirements and local initial fidelity thresholds. Building on this foundation, we extend to general quantum networks, where multiple paths may cross at common links. To this, we propose a heuristic approach, evaluate it through simulations, and compare its performance with a benchmark, a numerical approach and theoretical bounds, confirming the analytical ordering of their performance.
item.dc:creator: Vinay Kumar, Claudio Cicconetti, Marco Conti, Andrea Passarella

item.title: Apple Neural Engine: Architecture, Programming, and Performance
item.description: arXiv:2606.22283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is Apple's fixed-function matrix accelerator. It has shipped in every Apple system-on-chip since the A11 in iPhones and iPads and the M1 in Macs. Applications reach it only through Core ML, which documents almost nothing below its own surface. This work reverse-engineers the engine. We reach it directly, below Core ML, from an ordinary user process, and that access opens the rest to measurement. We measure on Apple silicon and decompile the private runtime, compiler, kernel driver, and firmware, checking each against the other. We give the datapath and the roofline that bounds throughput and energy. Below that are the compiler and the program format it emits, the weight-compression scheme, the kernel driver, the firmware, and the command protocol. We decode compiler targets for the A11 through A18 and M1 through M5 families, with per-chip tables and an operation-by-device matrix. We measured silicon on the M1 and M5 only, and we mark every claim measured, decompile-derived, or predicted. We record how we reached the engine and what we could not measure. The route is callable from user space, but Apple does not document or support it, and it breaks across operating-system updates. It serves measurement and on-device research. Core ML remains the path for shipped software.
item.dc:creator: Spencer H. Bryngelson

item.title: FAME: An FPGA-Based Platform for Approximate Multipliers Evaluation with Pattern-Guided DNN Retraining
item.description: arXiv:2609.17730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Approximate multipliers can reduce hardware area and energy consumption in Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference; however, they introduce computational errors. Assessing the accuracy of numerous approximate multiplier designs across diverse DNN models and large-scale datasets remains challenging due to prohibitive evaluation times. This overhead primarily stems from the slow emulation of approximate multiplier behavior using look-up tables (LUTs) on CPU and GPU platforms. Moreover, the resulting accuracy degradation must be carefully quantified and, if necessary, mitigated (e.g., through retraining), further increasing the overall evaluation cost. To address these challenges, we propose FAME, an FPGA-based platform for evaluating approximate multipliers. The platform exploits the reconfigurable logic of Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) to implement approximate multipliers directly in hardware, eliminating the need for LUT-based emulation on CPU/GPU platforms and thereby enabling efficient DNN inference while significantly reducing evaluation time on large datasets. Furthermore, we introduce a pattern-guided DNN retraining technique to mitigate accuracy degradation induced by approximate multipliers. Specifically, retraining is guided by multiplier-specific patterns to effectively recover potential accuracy losses. We evaluate FAME using two DNN models, ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2, on the ImageNet dataset across 27 approximate multipliers. During inference, our approach achieves up to a 3.47x speedup in approximate multiplier evaluation compared to prior LUT-based emulation methods. Furthermore, the proposed retraining technique improves accuracy by up to 65.5% over existing retraining approaches for the evaluated multipliers. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/gicLAB/FAME
item.dc:creator: Rappy Saha, Nima Amirafshar, Jude Haris, Nima Taherinejad, Jos\'e Cano
